title: Why do some 70s film soundtracks just have one song?

commenti.body: Regardless of any downvotes to your post, I think I kind of ‘understand’ what you mean based on some of the films you mentioned. I’m far from a film scholar, but I regularly watch films even from back in the 1930s to today, so what this is only an opinion. Up until the late 1950s and early 1960s, the general trend is that your film score should be an orchestral piece, generally following traditional techniques for ‘accompanying music’ that go back to operas, symphonic poems, rhapsodies and other ‘narrative’ based music forms. Big band jazz and other variations also played an important role in it. But from the late 1950s onwards we start seeing more unconventional approaches to film score. For instance, Louis Malle’s Ascenseur pour l’échafaud (1958) had Miles Davis basically improvising over the score he wrote and was entirely recorded in a single session. Orchestration also changed to include modern and also less conventional instruments (like the Jaw Harp you mentioned). This is in line with late developments in the field of music more or less at that same time, with movements such as musique concrète (Edgar Varese and others), minimalism (Phillip Glass and others) and so on. Back in cinema, mix that with the developments of the french new wave, which also challenged established conventions in pacing, editing, narrative (and music, of course), and you have the ground laid for the experimentalism that thrived in the 1970s with italian Giallo and westerns, Jodorowsky’s Holy Mountain, and many others. So with many conventions broken, there’s nothing really remarkable about a filmmaker, back at that time, chosing a more minimalist approach to its film score, having one main theme and focusing on it. This can result in a more memorable experience, but also it can be because the crew really liked that one song. Sergio Leone liked Morricone’s Deborah’s Theme so much for his Once Upon a Time in America that he had that one song playing in the backgroung over and over while recording the scenes (and I can’t blame him, it’s also my favorite Morricone piece).

In the examples you mention I’d imagine it’s primarily budget, especially when you’re commissioning work from an artist. But also you could get away with having a “theme song” or no score at all more in those days.

Thank you for your kind and thorough reply. These two stood out for me bc *Suspiria* was played painfully loud (I wasn't alone in covering my ears) and *Sicilian Clan* repeatedly undercut any emotional catharsis with that goofy harp.

Giallo, spaghetti westerns, and other Italian genre fare of the era were always pretty low budget, getting by on Italians' ability to offer maximum style on the cheap.  Dialogue in, traditional Italian fashion, always dubbed after the fact. The scores often had a couple really cool songs or themes that they blasted you with non-stop, but the great thing was that even bottom of the barrel stuff like Joe d'amato softcore porn often had a few killer tracks.

The main theme from Suspiria imo is one of the coolest compositions ever created for film. To be frank, I can't remember the rest of the score, but it seems like the OST has about 9 songs, which is way below most Hollywood scores, which have the composer compose the score after the film is made, gearing it exactly to what is going on in the edit at any moment. As far as the Morricone one, the dude scored over 400 films, they weren't all getting his A game. He also does love him a good Jew's harp.

Is it the same song or different versions of the same song? Well you're wrong about Suspiria. Goblin did the entire soundtrack, what you're thinking of is a main theme. These still exist.


When Easy Rider came out and was stuffed to the brim with popular music, the movie and music industry went nuts. Musicals weren't the only kind of movie that could have music in it - who knew?


Selling an LP with a ton of songs from a movie was a win-win-win. Labels get paid, studios get paid, singers get paid. 


Movies outside of the studio system, or, God forbid, a foreign picture, didn't have the luxury of digging through the entire Warner music archive, so they had to compromise. Either you get a band to do the whole soundtrack, i.e. Goblin with Suspiria, or you get one song and use that as your main theme, think Midnight Cowboy and the fifty times we find out that everybody's talking at him.
What's a Jew's harp? I've heard of a jaw harp but never this.
It's the same thing. I believe jew's harp was the more common term until recently.

This is exactly what the post made me think of! That song was stuck in my head for a while afterward, so good! And the mariachi version also stuck out particularly to me, really unique and funny. I need to rewatch

I remember the first time I watched it I didn't even catch it until well into the movie, all the versions were different, and so many are diegetic I just accepted it. Ditto realizing there's no music in No Country for Old Men, I don't think I even noticed on a first watch.

I prefer saying jew's harp because i think it sounds funny. It's not really a derogatory term, but some people think it sounds non-PC these days, hence the recent switch.

Morricone, Umiliani, Ortaloni, Trovajoli, Lesiman, and many more would simply do riffs on the initial arrangement and make the theme song nuanced for differing scenes of differing emotions... 

It was creating uniformity across the score as something cohesive that tied the film together.
It took me a few rewatches and then it hit me during the grocery store scene. I think I’ll need to rewatch the Big Sleep and this in Chandler’s order next month.
